query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs) used in harsh corrosive mechanical environments, the key to simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance is the in‐situ formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline, passivated surface layer. This layer forms dynamically during mechanical loading, which refines the grain structure and promotes the development of a dense, uniform oxide film, thereby reducing defect density and impeding both mechanical material loss (wear) and electrochemical attack (corrosion).
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single–phase high-entropy alloy with a conventional, relatively coarse grain structure and standard passive film formation characteristics.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA sample to controlled sliding wear in a chloride-rich aqueous environment (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl) that induces mechanical deformation; this varied loading environment is expected to trigger dynamic grain refinement at the surface.
generation.conditions: Tests performed at room temperature in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution under identical sliding wear conditions (e.g., constant load and speed) for comparison, ensuring that mechanical deformation coupled with an aggressive corrosive medium is active.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra–nanocrystalline, passivated near–surface layer (featuring refined grains and a compact, stable oxide film) during the tribocorrosion process.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical stress induces localized plastic deformation that leads to dynamic grain refinement (or even amorphization) at the surface. This refined structure enhances rapid diffusion and uniform formation of a chemically stable passive oxide film. The resulting layer minimizes defects that typically serve as initiation sites for both wear and corrosion, thus lowering both degradation rates concurrently.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline HEA sample with a pre–annealed, coarse grain structure (i.e., one that does not form a dynamic nano-layer), the dynamically nanostructured HEA will show significantly lower wear rates and reduced corrosion current densities. In a coupled tribocorrosion test, the overall degradation will be less than the sum of individual wear and corrosion processes observed in the coarse–grained control.
generation.baseline: An identical HEA composition sample engineered to maintain a coarse grain structure (e.g., via pre–annealing or alloy stabilization that suppresses dynamic refinement), resulting in a standard passive film without the benefit of a refined surface layer.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate under conditions where the environment supports passive oxide formation (i.e., in oxidative, chloride–containing aqueous environments) and where the applied mechanical loading is sufficient to induce surface grain refinement. The beneficial effect may fail or be negligible in inert or non–oxidizing environments, or if the mechanical loading is insufficient to trigger the necessary surface transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in wear and corrosion resistance may vary with alloy composition, degree of deformation, and specific environmental parameters. Further experimental work is needed to determine the optimal conditions and material configurations that maximize the formation and protective effectiveness of the surface nanolayer.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples of identical composition. One set should be pre–treated (e.g., through annealing or alloying modifications) to maintain a coarse grain structure that resists dynamic surface refinement. The other set should be untreated to allow for normal deformation-induced grain refinement under wear. Subject both sets to the same tribocorrosion test in 3.5 wt% NaCl under controlled sliding conditions. Use surface imaging (SEM/TEM) and electrochemical measurements to assess the formation of a nanocrystalline passive layer, wear rates, and corrosion parameters over time.
measurements: Surface grain size and oxide film uniformity (via SEM/TEM)
Corrosion parameters (corrosion current density, polarization resistance via potentiodynamic polarization and EIS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coarse-grained (pre-treated) control sample shows similar or improved wear and corrosion resistance compared to the untreated, dynamically refined sample—that is, if the expected ultra–nanocrystalline passive layer does not provide a measurable benefit—the hypothesis that dynamic surface refinement governs simultaneous resistance to wear and corrosion is falsified.

Effect of Thermal Shock on Properties of a Strongly Amorphous AlCrTiZrMo High-Entropy Alloy Film

Abstract: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding

Abstract: To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
